card.tagline: Interlinked arms in an ever-open circle.
card.profile: Amis/Pangcah malikoda at the Ilisin harvest festival; age-graded circle.
card.profile_long: The Amis harvest dance, known locally as part of the Ilisin, Kiloma'an, or Malalikid ceremonies, is a foundational ritual held annually in Taiwan. The festival typically occurs in July, August, or September, following the rice harvest. The duration of the celebration varies by tribe, ranging from a single day to seven days. The dance is performed by men and women of all ages, who gather in circles to pray to ancestral gods for successful crops, population growth, and stock breeding. The dance is not merely a performance but a medium for communicating with the soul of the ancestors and the divine. The structure of the dance is communal, with participants holding hands to form a circle, a formation believed to keep 'bad souls' away from the gathering. The movements are characterized by walking, running, and jumping. In coastal areas, these movements are noted as being more complex and changeable than those found in mountainous regions, with the 'Makotaay' being a representative dance form near harbor areas. The dance is led by a soloist, with a chorus of participants following. The songs are considered serious and unchangeable, with lyrics that reflect the realities of fishing and farming. The festival also serves as a critical social stage. Elders sit in the center of the circle, observing the youth as they dance and propose toasts. This interaction allows elders to evaluate young men for potential tribal leadership. Simultaneously, the dance acts as a courtship ritual. On the final night, young men dance with bags on their backs; women join the circle and place betel nuts into the bags of the men they wish to partner with. If the sentiment is mutual, the man gives his bag to the woman, marking the beginning of a couple. The participants wear traditional festival clothing, including hats decorated with rooster feathers, where the number of feathers indicates the individual's status within the tribe. The ceremony is overseen by a priest, who is responsible for the sacrificial rituals and possesses deep knowledge of the calendar, weather, and tribal history.
card.sacred_note: The songs and rituals are serious and unchangeable, serving as a medium for communicating with ancestors and gods; outsiders should observe with respect and follow local guidance regarding participation.

sections.origins_and_history: The festival is held after the rice harvest, though it was historically tied to the reaping of millet. It is a time for ancestral worship and the strengthening of tribal bonds.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Participants dance hand-in-hand in a circle. The primary movements consist of walking, running, and jumping. The dance is led by a soloist who initiates the singing, with the rest of the group following in a chorus.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is vocal-based, consisting of a lead singer and a chorus. The songs are described as serious and unchangeable, serving as a medium for spiritual communication.
sections.costume_and_setting: Participants wear festival-specific clothing. A key element is the hat, which is decorated with rooster feathers; the quantity of feathers denotes the wearer's status within the tribe.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed during the Ilisin Harvest Festival. It serves to honor ancestors, celebrate the harvest, facilitate partner selection, and allow elders to identify future leaders.
sections.notable_figures: The tribal priest, who is a knowledgeable and wise man responsible for instructing agricultural activities and sacrificial rituals.
sections.regional_variants: Dancing styles vary by location. Coastal tribes generally perform more complex and changeable movements compared to those in mountainous areas. The 'Makotaay' is a specific representative dance of harbor-area tribes.
sections.lineage: An indigenous tradition of the Amis people in Taiwan, passed down through generations as part of the age-structure-based social system.

claims.text: The “Harvest Festival”, also known as the “Harvest Ceremony”, is one of the most important festival for indigenous tribes in Taiwan and it is held to celebrate the harvest.
At that time, the men and women, the young and old wearing festival costumes, led by a singer, dance with hand in hand.
The movements in the dance are mostly walking, running and jumping.
The songs are regarded as the media through which the people communicate with the soul of the ancestors and the god.
The form of the singing is that one person leads a chorus and others follow.
They will wear hats which are decorated with the feathers of roosters and the number of the feather symbols the status of the one in the tribe.
The Amis Harvest Festival is held on the full moon day after the autumn harvest.
